note.explanation: Matter occurs in different states. The particle arrangement, distance between particles and strength of attractions explain how solids, liquids, gases and plasma behave.
examples: Ice is a solid: its particles are closely packed and stay around fixed positions.
Air is a gas: its particles are far apart, so it is easy to compress.
note.checkAnswer: Gases have particles that are very widely apart, no order whatsoever and very weak intermolecular forces.
note.simple: Think of particles as tiny pieces. In a solid they are tightly packed, in a liquid they stay close but move around, and in a gas they are far apart.
note.title: States of Matter
steps: Compare how close the particles are.
Compare how freely the particles can move.
Use the particle arrangement and attractions to explain the state’s properties.
note.answer: Matter can exist as a solid, liquid, gas or plasma, as well as in less commonly encountered states.

options: It has a definite shape and fixed volume.
It is easily compressed because its particles are far apart.
Its particles are close together but move randomly.
It consists of particles with very high kinetic energy.

rationales: This is correct because solids have a definite shape and fixed volume.
This describes a gas, whose widely spaced particles make it easily compressible.
This describes a liquid, whose closely attached particles move randomly.
This describes plasma, which is composed of particles with very high kinetic energy.

written.text: Q1.4. Both graphite and graphene have hexagonal layered structures. What is the difference?
written.finalAnswer: Graphite has many layers of carbon atoms, whereas graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern.

rubric.why: Identifying graphite’s layered structure makes the comparison clear.
rubric.description: State that graphite consists of many layers.
rubric.how: Mention that graphite has multiple layers of carbon atoms.

rubric.why: The key structural difference is that graphene is one layer.
rubric.description: State that graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms.
rubric.how: Mention its single layer and hexagonal arrangement.

modelAnswer: Graphite has many layers of carbon atoms.
Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern.
Therefore, graphite has many layers, whereas graphene has only one.

written.text: Q1.5. Why are supercritical fluids important?
written.finalAnswer: Supercritical fluids show both properties of gases and liquids, so reactions that may not be carried out in conventional solvents may possibly be carried out in supercritical carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: Their combined gas-like and liquid-like properties explain their importance.
rubric.description: State that they show properties of both gases and liquids.
rubric.how: Name both kinds of properties.

rubric.why: The section gives a possible use in carrying out otherwise difficult reactions.
rubric.description: Give the example of reactions in supercritical carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Explain that reactions not possible in conventional solvents may possibly be carried out in it.

modelAnswer: Supercritical fluids are highly compressed states which show both properties of gases and liquids.
Chemical reactions which may not be carried out in conventional solvents may possibly be carried out in supercritical carbon dioxide.
Therefore, supercritical fluids are important as they may be used to carry out such reactions.

written.text: Q1.6. In which state does matter exist in the Sun?

rubric.why: The correct state is needed to answer the question.
rubric.description: Name the state of matter.
rubric.how: Write plasma.

rubric.why: A clear final statement makes the answer unambiguous.
rubric.description: Give the answer clearly.
rubric.how: State that matter in the Sun exists as plasma.

modelAnswer: Matter in the Sun exists in the plasma state.
Therefore, the answer is plasma.

written.text: Q1.7. What is the importance of graphene?
written.finalAnswer: Graphene is a tough, flexible and light material with high resistance.

rubric.why: These are important properties specifically stated in the section.
rubric.description: Name graphene’s toughness and flexibility.
rubric.how: Include that it is tough and flexible.

rubric.why: The section also identifies its lightness and resistance as useful properties.
rubric.description: Name its lightness and high resistance.
rubric.how: Include that it is light and has high resistance.

modelAnswer: Graphene is a tough, flexible and light material with a high resistance.
These properties make graphene an important material.

written.text: Q1.8. Which form of matter do most of the material things in this world belong to?

rubric.why: The question asks for the form of matter most material things belong to.
rubric.description: Identify the state.
rubric.how: Answer solid.

rubric.why: A complete statement makes the answer clear.
rubric.description: State the answer as a form of matter.
rubric.how: Write that most material things belong to the solid state.

modelAnswer: Most material things in this world belong to the solid state.
Therefore, the answer is the solid state.

written.text: Q1.1. How does a supercritical state look like?
written.finalAnswer: A supercritical fluid is a highly compressed state that shows both properties of gases and liquids.

rubric.why: The high compression is a defining feature of the description in the section.
rubric.description: Describe the state as highly compressed.
rubric.how: Use the phrase highly compressed.

rubric.why: The gas-like properties are part of what characterises the state.
rubric.description: Mention gas properties.
rubric.how: State that it shows properties of gases.

rubric.why: The liquid-like properties complete the comparison.
rubric.description: Mention liquid properties.
rubric.how: State that it also shows properties of liquids.

rubric.why: The final answer must combine compression with both types of properties.
rubric.description: Give the complete description.
rubric.how: Explain that it is highly compressed and shows properties of gases and liquids.

modelAnswer: Supercritical fluids are highly compressed states.
They show properties of gases.
They also show properties of liquids.
Therefore, a supercritical fluid is a highly compressed state that shows both properties of gases and liquids.

written.text: Q1.2. In what way is plasma created in a fluorescent tube?
written.finalAnswer: Electrical energy ionizes the gas in the tube, producing plasma containing electrons and ions.

rubric.why: An energy source is needed to explain how the gas becomes ionized.
rubric.description: Identify the electrical energy supplied to the tube.
rubric.how: Mention electricity or electrical energy.

rubric.why: Plasma forms from the gas inside the tube.
rubric.description: Identify the gas in the tube as the material that changes.
rubric.how: Say that the gas in the tube is affected.

rubric.why: Ionization is the process that produces the partially ionized gas.
rubric.description: Explain that the gas becomes ionized.
rubric.how: Use ionizes or an equivalent form of the word.

rubric.why: The final statement should identify the resulting plasma and charged particles.
rubric.description: State that plasma containing charged particles is formed.
rubric.how: Name plasma and include electrons and ions.

modelAnswer: Electrical energy is supplied to the gas in the fluorescent tube.
The energy ionizes the gas.
The partially ionized gas contains electrons and ions.
Therefore, plasma is created in the fluorescent tube.

written.text: Q1.3. What are supercritical fluids. How are they different from ordinary liquids?
written.finalAnswer: Supercritical fluids are highly compressed states that show both properties of gases and liquids. Ordinary liquids do not have the combined properties described for supercritical fluids.

rubric.why: This is the defining description of supercritical fluids in the section.
rubric.description: Define supercritical fluids as highly compressed states.
rubric.how: Include the phrase highly compressed.

rubric.why: Their gas-like and liquid-like properties distinguish them.
rubric.description: State that they show properties of both gases and liquids.
rubric.how: Mention both gases and liquids.

rubric.why: A comparison with ordinary liquids is required by the question.
rubric.description: Make a clear comparison with ordinary liquids.
rubric.how: Name ordinary liquids in the comparison.

rubric.why: The final comparison must express the combined nature of the supercritical state.
rubric.description: Conclude with the distinguishing combined properties.
rubric.how: Explain that supercritical fluids show both gas and liquid properties.

modelAnswer: Supercritical fluids are highly compressed states.
They show both properties of gases and liquids.
Ordinary liquids do not show this combination of gas and liquid properties.
Therefore, supercritical fluids differ from ordinary liquids by showing properties of both gases and liquids.

written.text: Q1.5. What types of movements are present in gaseous and liquid molecules?
written.finalAnswer: Gas molecules move freely and are very widely apart; liquid molecules are closely attached but move randomly.

rubric.why: The description of gas particles helps distinguish their movement and arrangement.
rubric.description: Describe the spacing of gas molecules.
rubric.how: State that they are very widely apart.

rubric.why: Gas molecules have freedom to move in the widely spaced arrangement.
rubric.description: Describe gas molecule movement.
rubric.how: Say that they move freely or randomly.

rubric.why: Close attachment is a key feature of liquid molecules.
rubric.description: Describe how closely liquid molecules are held.
rubric.how: State that they are closely attached.

rubric.why: Random movement is the movement specifically stated for liquid molecules.
rubric.description: Describe liquid molecule movement.
rubric.how: State that they move randomly.

modelAnswer: Gas molecules are very widely apart and move freely.
Liquid molecules are closely attached but move randomly.
Therefore, gaseous molecules move freely, while liquid molecules move randomly while remaining close together.

written.text: Q1.2. Graphene is called a miracle material and it is the material of the future. Which of its many properties makes it very useful in electronics?
written.finalAnswer: Graphene’s high electrical conductivity makes it useful in electronics.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the material being discussed.

rubric.how: Make the answer explicitly about graphene.

rubric.why: Electrical conductivity is the property that makes graphene useful for electronic applications.
rubric.description: Identify its electrical conductivity.
rubric.how: Mention conductivity or that it conducts electricity.

rubric.why: The property must be connected to the use asked about.
rubric.description: Link the property to electronics.
rubric.how: State that the property makes it useful in electronics.

rubric.why: The final answer should give the material, property and application together.
rubric.description: Give the complete property-use connection.
rubric.how: Conclude that graphene’s electrical conductivity makes it useful in electronics.

modelAnswer: Graphene has high electrical conductivity.
Electrical conductivity is useful in electronic applications.
Therefore, graphene’s high electrical conductivity makes it useful in electronics.

examTips: Board questions commonly ask you to compare solids, liquids and gases using particle spacing, arrangement, movement, intermolecular forces and compressibility.
For state-identification questions, connect the example to the correct state: fluorescent tubes and lightning are examples of plasma.
For short answers, give the state or definition first, then add the property or example asked for.
In comparison questions, write a separate, accurate feature for each state; this makes the marking points easy to identify.

example.question: Use the textbook’s description to explain why gases are easily compressible and have low densities.
example.answer: Gas molecules are very widely apart, have no order whatsoever and have very weak intermolecular forces. These features make gases easily compressible, and their densities are very low.

explain.title: What matter and a state of matter mean
explain.body: Your textbook defines matter as: “Anything other than energy which carries weight and occupies volume is called matter.” It defines a state of matter as: “A state of matter is one of the many distinct forms in which matter can exist.” The four states observed in everyday life are solid, liquid, gas and plasma.

explain.title: Solids, liquids and gases
explain.body: Solids have a definite shape and fixed volume; their particles are closely packed and can oscillate about their mean positions. Liquid molecules are closely attached but move randomly. Gas molecules are very widely apart, have no order whatsoever and have very weak intermolecular forces, so gases are easily compressible and have very low densities.

explain.title: Plasma and other states
explain.body: Your textbook defines plasma as: “Plasma can be considered as a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions, photons, etc.” It gives fluorescent tubes, lightning and welding arcs as examples. Supercritical fluids show properties of both gases and liquids. Liquid crystals have properties between conventional liquids and crystalline solids.

explain.title: Graphene and exotic states
explain.body: Graphene is a two-dimensional crystal: a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern. The section describes it as tough, flexible and light, with a high resistance. States not commonly encountered are called exotic states of matter; examples include dark matter and Bose-Einstein condensate.

mistakes: Do not say gas molecules are close together; the text says they are very widely apart.
Do not say solid particles are completely motionless: they can oscillate about their mean positions.
Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas; plasma is described as a partially ionized gas.
Do not confuse graphene with liquid crystal: graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, while liquid crystal properties are between those of conventional liquids and crystalline solids.
When describing supercritical fluids, include both gas and liquid properties, not just one of them.
